paragraphs.text: Lesson 19, the times are changing.
Noel is looking for a job, but he's not having much success.
His friend Tori tries to give him support and advice.
Listen to their conversation and mark these statements as true or false.
Hey Noel, you're looking sharp today, but why the long face?
I just got back from a job interview, and it was nothing but a waste of time.
Sorry to hear that.
Was this the RN job at Medical Alliance?
Yep.
What happened? I thought you were a shoe-in for that position.
So did I.
Well, this morning I made sure my resume was flawless and headed out the door in high spirits.
That's a good way to approach a job interview.
I figured I had the job in the bag.
I've got a solid background in nursing.
My last employer gave me a great reference.
Heck, I even graduated at the top of my nursing class.
But was that enough to make the cut?
Mmm, you didn't get the job, I take it.
Bingo.
And absolutely insufferable kid named Mitch interviewed me.
He took one glance at my resume, then tossed it aside.
It seemed like he couldn't care less about my experience.
No way. So what did he ask you?
Not much at all.
Actually, he spent most of the interview rambling about the future of medical care.
And every time I tried to bring up my strong points, he cut me off.
I've had interviews with people like that.
Real know-it-alls who just want to put you down while making themselves look important and smart.
They just like to hear themselves talk.
According to him, I'm not what medical alliance is looking for at the current time.
He said they need bright and forward-thinking nurses who can adapt to the ever-changing medical world.
And in his point of view, you didn't fit the bill, huh?
I really think he rejected me because of my gray hair.
Look, I'm no spring chicken.
But I know they're ropes when it comes to nursing.
It seems like experiencing qualifications aren't enough anymore.
Exactly. These young folks just see me as being out of date and out of touch with the modern world.
I'm so sorry, Noel. The world is constantly changing. People are changing. Times aren't like they used to be.
When I started out, all you needed to get your foot in the door were training and skills.
But now it's a whole new ballgame. I have to try extra hard to come across as innovative and dynamic.
I know what you mean. I work in the music industry, and if I don't keep up with the latest trends, I'll get the axe in a heartbeat.
Job security is a thing of the past.
How am I even supposed to find a job when these stuck-up HR managers won't hire perfectly capable nurses?
Don't lose heart, Noel. You'd be a great asset to any hospital. I'll keep an eye out for any job opportunities.
Thanks, Tori. I appreciate it.
Alright, let's learn the vocabulary from Tori and Noel's conversation.
Tori says that Noel is looking sharp. Looking sharp means looking good, well-dressed.
But she asks, why the long face? This is an idiom which means why are you sad or why are you upset.
Noel interviewed for an RN job. RN stands for registered nurse. And Tori thought he was a shoe-in for that position.
A shoe-in is a person who is certain to be selected.
Noel explains what happened. First, he made sure his resume was flawless. The word flawless means perfect.
And he headed out the door in high spirits. The phrasal verb head out is an informal way to say leave.
And in high spirits means he was happy or joyful.
Noel figured he had the job in the bag. This expression means he thought he would definitely get the job.
And Noel had great qualifications, but it wasn't enough to make the cut.
Make the cut means be good enough to be accepted, according to a standard which will include some people and exclude others.
Tori replies, you didn't get the job I take it. I take it means I assume, I guess or understand.
Noel didn't say directly that he didn't get the job, but he implied it. So, Tori makes an assumption, you didn't get the job I take it.
Noel replies, bingo. Bingo is slang, meaning you're exactly right. Then Noel explains.
An absolutely insufferable kid named Mitch interviewed me.
The word insufferable means impossible to tolerate. We use this word for a really annoying person.
The interviewer took one glance at Noel's resume, then tossed it aside.
Took one glance means he looked at it very briefly, very quickly. Then he tossed it aside.
This means he casually put or threw it to the side.
It seemed like the interviewer couldn't care less about Noel's experience.
Couldn't care less means he completely didn't care.
Noel then describes the interview. He says that Mitch spent most of the interview rambling about the future of medical care.
The verb rambling means talking too long with too many details.
Every time Noel tried to bring up his strong points, the interviewer cut him off.
In this sentence we have two phrasal verbs.
Bring up means to introduce a topic in conversation. So, Noel was trying to bring up his strong points.
He was trying to talk about his strong points. But the interviewer cut him off.
To cut somebody off in a conversation means to interrupt the person and not let them speak.
Tori's also experienced similar interviews. She says those people are real know-it-alls.
A know-it-all is a person who thinks he or she is intellectually superior and knows everything.
According to Tori, these people just want to put you down while making themselves look important and smart.
The phrasal verb put someone down means to make that person feel inferior.
Noel said the interviewer was looking for bright and forward-thinking nurses.
The word bright is another way to say intelligent, and forward-thinking describes someone innovative who thinks about the future
and is not limited by an old-fashioned's perspective.
In the interviewer's opinion, Noel didn't fit the bill.
Didn't fit the bill means not suitable for what is required.
Noel admits that he's no spring chicken.
No spring chicken means he's not a young person. He's a little bit older.
But he says, I know the ropes when it comes to nursing.
If you know the ropes, it means you know an area very well. You know how to do something properly.
According to Noel, these young folks just see me as being out of date and out of touch with the modern world.
The word folks is an informal way to say people, and out of touch means not informed about current developments.
Noel says that when he started out, all you needed to get your foot in the door were training and skills.
To get your foot in the door means to gain access or entry to an opportunity, especially a career.
But now he says it's a whole new ball game.
The expression a whole new ball game means it's a completely different situation or set of circumstances.
For example, you have to try extra hard to come across as innovative and dynamic.
Come across as means to make an impression of being a certain way.
Tori says she works in the music industry, and if she doesn't keep up with the latest trends, she'll get the axe in a heartbeat.
Get the axe is a slang way to say get fired, lose your job, and in a heartbeat means very fast almost immediately.
Noel complains that he can't even find a job when there are stuck-up HR managers who won't hire perfectly capable nurses.
The word stuck-up is an informal way to say arrogant.
But Tori tries to encourage him. She says don't lose heart, Noel.
Don't lose heart means don't become discouraged.
Tori then offers to keep an eye out for any job opportunities.
To keep an eye out for something means watch to see if that thing appears.
So hopefully Noel will be able to find a position that values his skills and experience.
That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation.
